# A morning

In 1446, the *Hunminjeongeum* introduced Hangeul (한글), the Korean alphabet. It
opened by stating the entire system in a few pages: every letter, and the rules
for combining letters. The explanations came only after those pages. The book's
postface promised that the letters were quick to learn: *a wise man can learn
the letters before the morning is over.*

This part of the book makes the same promise. It is short on purpose,
so that you can finish it in a single reading. It holds a first plot, then gog's whole vocabulary in
one table, then practice. The practice has two halves: first reading finished
sentences, then writing your own. The second half also shows the refusals you
are most likely to see.

This part covers each idea only briefly. Nearly every idea you meet here has a
full chapter later in the book. Instead, this part teaches three skills. When you
finish it, you should be able to read any gog sentence, in this book or in a
colleague's script. You should also be able to write a sentence that answers
your own question, and to predict whether gog will draw that sentence or
refuse it.
